A neti pot is a small container, shaped roughly like a tiny teapot or a genie lamp, designed specifically for rinsing the inside of your nose with a saline (saltwater) solution. The long, narrow spout is shaped to fit snugly into a nostril.

Your nose and sinuses (the hollow spaces behind your nose and cheeks) are passages through which air flows. These passages can collect mucus, dust, pollen, bacteria, and other irritants. A neti pot lets you literally wash these passages out with a gentle stream of saltwater — the same way you might rinse dirt from a wound.

You fill the neti pot with a prepared saline solution, tilt your head sideways over a sink, insert the spout into your upper nostril, and let gravity do the work. The water flows in through one nostril, travels through your nasal cavity, and drains out through the other nostril. You breathe through your mouth the entire time. You then repeat on the other side.

The salt in the water is important — plain water would irritate your nasal lining. Saline closely matches the natural fluid concentration of your body tissues, so it is gentle and well-tolerated.

People use neti pots to:

  • Relieve nasal congestion caused by colds, flu, or sinusitis (inflammation of the sinuses).
  • Manage allergies — rinsing out pollen, dust mites, pet dander, and other allergens reduces allergic symptoms like a runny or stuffy nose.
  • Thin and clear thick mucus, which helps with sinus pressure and headaches.
  • Flush out irritants after being in a dusty, smoky, or polluted environment.
  • Daily nasal hygiene, as a preventive practice, especially common in Ayurvedic wellness traditions from India where this technique originates.

Doctors and ENT specialists (ear, nose, and throat doctors) often recommend nasal irrigation with a neti pot as a drug-free, evidence-backed complement to treating chronic sinusitis and allergies.

This is arguably the most important thing to know about neti pots: you must never use plain tap water directly from the tap.

Tap water contains microscopic organisms that are completely harmless when you drink them — your stomach acid kills them. But when you pour water directly into your nasal passages, it bypasses those defenses. Rare but dangerous organisms like the amoeba Naegleria fowleri can travel up into the brain through the nasal route and cause a fatal infection.

Always use one of these:

  • Distilled water (available in stores)
  • Sterile water (labeled as such)
  • Boiled tap water that has been allowed to cool to a lukewarm temperature

Beyond water safety, always use non-iodized salt (iodine can irritate the nasal lining), or a pre-made saline packet specifically designed for nasal irrigation.

Rinse the neti pot thoroughly after every use and let it air-dry completely before storing. A damp pot can grow bacteria and mold. Replace it regularly, especially if it shows any discoloration or cracks.

People with a deviated septum (when the wall between your two nostrils is off-center) may find water flows unevenly or not at all. People with ear infections or eardrum perforations should avoid neti pot use, as fluid can travel toward the ears through the Eustachian tubes. If you have any such condition, check with a doctor first.

Children can use neti pots, but adult supervision and appropriately-sized child versions are recommended.

A neti pot is a simple, drug-free hygiene tool that uses the power of gravity and saltwater to physically wash out your nasal passages — clearing congestion, flushing allergens, and promoting healthier breathing. Used correctly (with safe water and clean equipment), it is safe, effective, and widely endorsed by medical professionals for nasal and sinus care.
